## Linear Regression

Remember that linear regression is $E[Y_i|X_i] = \beta_0 +\beta_1*x_i$ and requires
1. Linearity 
2. E[\espilon] = 0
3. \V(\epsilon)=\sigma^2
4. \epsilon_i \perpendicular \epsilon_j
5. \epsilon ~\norm(0,\sigma^2)

### Testing usefullness
The deviance is TSS = \sum_{(y_i - \bar{mean})^2}
SSR =  \sum_{(\hat(y_i) - \bar{y_i})^2}
SSE =  \sum_{(y_i - \bar{y_i})^2}

It can be decomposed as
SS = \sum_{y_i-\bar{mean}} = \sum_{(\hat(y_i) - \bar{y_i})^2} + \sum_{(y_i - \bar{y_i})^2}

to test we use F-statistics which is the ratio of
1. the explained variability
2. the unexplained variability

We have
TSS/\sigma^2 * (n-1)/\sigma^2 = s^2*(n-1)/\sigma^2 ~ \Xi^2_(n-1)
SSR/\sigma^2 * (p-1)/(p-1) ~ \Xi^2_(p-1)
SSE/\sigma^2 * (n-p)/(n-p) ~ \Xi^2_(n-p)

Dividing we have
TSS-SSE/SST = (R^2/p-1)/((1-R2)/(n-p)) ~ \fisher_(p-1),(n-p)

Note: if you square the t-statistic then you get F-statistic if you have 1 parameter

### Model checking
You use the residuals of : e_i = y_i - \bar{y_i} (not that they are not errors \epsilon, but can be considered their realisation?what does realisation mean?)
You want this to be as close to 0 as possible and variability to be constant

plotting the red-line should be almost straight and, drawing 2 imaginary lines, the interval should be costant (variability)
the resisuals q-q plot should also follow a normal distribution
Residuals vs leverage will tell you the impact of influential values


Another way is evaluate the error (\epsilon) vs covariate:
e.g. seeing a curve, you can try to transform it by squaring the data -> \beta_0 + (\beta_1*x_i +) \beta_2*x_i^2
